title: Nightly: history, triage, mutation and the locks

story: Every night at 02:44 UTC fcp's cloud integration tests run against the shared QA environment, and every morning a Slack channel gets the same red message. It has failed sixty nights in a row, on AWS and on GCP. One night's log is 88 minutes long and says 4 failed, 312 passed and 4 reruns. Nobody opens it any more.

Then a change that breaks archiving a project is merged on a Tuesday. Wednesday's nightly fails because of it, and the message looks exactly like the fifty-nine messages before it. The nightly caught the bug, and nobody noticed, because red had stopped meaning anything.
hook.question: How do we make a red nightly mean something again, so people, and later agents, can act on it?

read.h: One red light hides four different stories
p: A night is reported as one result: green or red. Inside a red night there can be four very different kinds of failure. A real bug fails every night from the day it was merged. A flaky test, one that passes or fails on the same code depending on timing, fails on some nights and not others. A test that is retried until it passes looks green, so its flakiness is hidden completely. And when the environment itself breaks, for example a QA image that does not build, many tests fail on the same night for one reason that has nothing to do with the code.

You cannot tell these apart by looking at one night. You can tell them apart at a glance when you put the nights next to each other, one row per test and one column per night. A row that turns red on one date and stays red is a regression; you look at what was merged that day. A row with scattered red is flaky. A column that is red in many rows is the environment. So the first job is not to fix anything: it is to keep each night's per-test results.

read.h: Keep a JUnit file every night, and read reruns honestly
p: JUnit XML is the standard report format for test results that almost every test runner can write and almost every CI tool can read: one testcase element per test, with a failure element inside when it failed. pytest writes it with --junitxml=<file>. fcp's nightly runs its tests inside a Kubernetes pod through kubectl exec, so the report is written inside the pod; the job copies it out with kubectl cp before the step that deletes the pod, and uploads it as an artifact, a file GitHub keeps with the run, here for 90 days.

One detail decides whether the history tells the truth. Ten of fcp's integration tests carry @pytest.mark.flaky(reruns=N) from the pytest-rerunfailures plugin, which runs a failing test again up to N times. In the JUnit file each attempt becomes its own testcase element, and the failed attempts that were retried have no failure element at all. A script that reads every entry on its own counts those tests as green. So the history script groups the entries by test: the last entry is the verdict, and more than one entry means the test needed a rerun. A rerun pass is counted as flaky, not as green.

code.file: history.py (the lab version; fcp's is scripts/nightly_history.py)

notes.text: One JUnit file per night, newest first, so the newest night is the first column.
Group by test name: a rerun test appears once per attempt.
Only the last attempt is the verdict.
A quarantined test that failed shows up as skipped, with its ticket in the message.
Passed, but only after a rerun: flaky, not green.

read.h: Triage: fix, quarantine with a ticket, or hand over
p: With the table in front of them, the backend engineers go through every failing or rerun-only test once, together, and give each one a category and an owner. A real bug or a broken test is fixed at once if that takes under an hour, otherwise it gets a bug ticket with the failing output. An environment problem goes to DevOps, the team that owns the QA environments, with the evidence. A flaky test is quarantined.

Quarantine means the test keeps running and reporting every night, but its failure no longer turns the night red. It is not the same as deleting or skipping the test: the history still shows it, and the quarantine names a Jira ticket labelled flaky-test, which our flaky-test fixer (an agent routine that looks for the real cause of a flaky test and fixes it) can take. In pytest this is a small marker that turns into a non-strict xfail: pytest expects the test may fail, so a failure is reported as expected and a pass is fine too. Only people add the marker. An agent that quarantines, skips or deletes a test to make its own work green is exactly what the checks against weakened tests exist to catch.

Once the flaky tests are quarantined and the real bugs fixed, a red night means one thing again: something new broke. The team posts one line a week, green nights out of the last seven, so everyone can see whether it stays that way.

notes.text: Register the marker, so pytest accepts @pytest.mark.quarantine(ticket=...).
No quarantine without a ticket: a missing ticket is an error at collection.
Non-strict xfail: the test runs, a failure is expected, a pass is fine.

deeper.h: Go deeper: mutants, and QA leaves the branches
p: Green tests can still be weak tests. A nightly, advisory job runs mutmut, a mutation testing tool, on the cloud files that agent pull requests changed the day before, at most ten. mutmut makes small changes to the code on purpose, such as turning < into <=, and each change is a mutant. If the API tests still pass, the mutant survived, which shows a place where the tests do not really check the code. The job is never a required check; it publishes the survivors, and a routine that looks for test gaps turns them into proposals for new tests.

The nightly also becomes more important for another reason. Once the private FCP Lab smoke run (the full product on one machine, booted for one CI run) has run next to QA for two weeks and caught everything QA caught, branch pushes of cloud and client code stop waiting for the shared QA locks. QA then runs only on main, for releases and in the nightly, so the nightly is where QA-only problems show up first.

lab.title: Ten nights in one table
needs: No Docker and no CI: a loop plays ten nights
lab.goal: Run a small nightly ten times, turn the JUnit files into a per-test history that counts reruns honestly, and quarantine the flaky test with a ticket so the next night is green.

guess.q: test_upload_scan fails on its first attempt, is rerun by pytest-rerunfailures, and passes. What does the night's JUnit file show for it?

options.text: One entry with a failure, and one entry that passed.
options.why: That would be honest, but the plugin writes the retried attempt without a failure element.

options.text: Two entries for the same test, and neither has a failure element.
options.why: Each attempt is its own testcase. Only the count of entries shows that a rerun happened.

options.text: One entry that passed, with a rerun count.
options.why: There is no rerun attribute. The terminal summary shows reruns with -rR, the JUnit file only repeats the entry.

follow.do:
cat > tests/conftest.py <<'EOF'
import pytest


def pytest_configure(config: pytest.Config) -> None:
    config.addinivalue_line("markers", "quarantine(ticket): known flaky; still runs and reports, but cannot turn the night red")


def pytest_collection_modifyitems(items: list[pytest.Item]) -> None:
    for item in items:
        marker = item.get_closest_marker("quarantine")
        if marker is None:
            continue
        ticket = marker.kwargs["ticket"]  # required: every quarantined test has a ticket and an owner
        item.add_marker(pytest.mark.xfail(reason=f"quarantined, see {ticket}", strict=False))
EOF
python3 - <<'EOF'
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("tests/test_nightly.py")
s = p.read_text()
s = s.replace("def test_run_report():", '@pytest.mark.quarantine(ticket="RH-1251")\ndef test_run_report():')
s = s.replace("archived = NIGHT < 7  # on night 7 a change was merged that breaks archiving", "archived = True  # the archiving fix was merged")
p.write_text(s)
EOF
NIGHT=11 uv run pytest -q -rx -p no:cacheprovider --junitxml=nights/night-11.xml

lab.build: A quarantined test that passes is written to JUnit as a plain pass, so on good nights the history forgets it is quarantined, and nobody can list the quarantined tests and their tickets. Play NIGHT=12 to see it: test_run_report shows pass. Fix it in two places. In conftest.py, also add item.user_properties.append(("quarantined", ticket)), which pytest writes into JUnit as a property on every night. In history.py, check for that property first (last.find("properties/property[@name='quarantined']")), show quar whenever it is there, and print one line per quarantined test with its ticket under the table. Run night 12 again and read the history.
checks: Night 7's JUnit file lists test_upload_scan twice, without a failure element.
history.py shows rerun for test_upload_scan on nights 7, 8 and 10, and FAIL for test_archive_project from night 7.
After the quarantine, night 11 reports 3 passed, 1 xfailed, and the XFAIL line names RH-1251.
With your change, night 12 shows quar for test_run_report even though it passed, and the history prints quarantined: test_run_report (RH-1251).

explain: Why can one red night not tell you whether a failure is a regression, a flaky test or the environment, and what does the table show for each?
Why does a test that needed a rerun look green in the JUnit file, and how does history.py notice it?
How is a quarantined test different from a skipped or deleted one, and why may only a person add the marker?
lab.done: Your table shows the regression, the rerun-only flakiness and the quarantined test, night 11 is green, and the quarantine stays visible on nights it passes.

check.q: In the table, test_archive_project passes on nights 1 to 6 and fails on every night from 7 on. What is the most likely story?

options.text: It is flaky, so it should be quarantined.
options.why: Flaky tests fail on scattered nights. A clean switch from green to red on one date points at a change.

options.text: A change merged before night 7 broke it, so look at what was merged that day and fix it.
options.why: A regression starts on a date and stays. Quarantining it would hide a real bug.

options.text: The QA environment broke on night 7.
options.why: Then many tests would turn red on the same night, not one test alone.

check.q: Why is a test that passed only after a rerun counted as flaky and not as green?

options.text: Because it failed on the same code at least once, and the rerun only hid that.
options.why: Retrying until green makes flakiness invisible. Counting it keeps it in the history, where someone can fix the cause.

options.text: Because reruns make the nightly slower.
options.why: Speed is not the point. The point is what the result tells you about the test.

options.text: Because pytest marks reruns as failures in JUnit.
options.why: It does the opposite: the retried attempt has no failure element, which is why the script must count entries.

check.q: A pull request from an agent adds @pytest.mark.quarantine(ticket=...) to a test that its change made red. What should happen?

options.text: It is fine, because the test still runs and reports.
options.why: The test still runs, but the night stays green, so the agent's own change escapes its check.

options.text: It is fine if the ticket key is real.
options.why: A ticket does not change who made the decision. Quarantine is a person's call after triage.

options.text: The checks against weakened tests should reject it: only people quarantine tests.
options.why: An agent that can quarantine the test it broke can make any change look green.

p: In _cloud-int-tests-reusable-aws.yml and -gcp.yml, the entrypoint call inside kubectl exec gets -rR --junitxml=/tmp/junit.xml; a new step copies it out with kubectl cp -c integration-tests before "Delete the integration tests pod" and uploads nightly-junit-<cloud> with retention-days 90. scripts/nightly_history.py reads the last 20 scheduled runs (gh run list --workflow cloud-int-tests-dispatch.yml --event schedule -L 20, then gh run download -n nightly-junit-aws) and writes nightly-history.md; the frontend nightly follows later with Playwright's JUnit reporter.

Triage happens in one session with the BE guild. The quarantine marker is registered in cloud/rhinoCloud/pytest.ini and applied from the existing pytest_collection_modifyitems; each quarantined test, and each of the ten tests with @pytest.mark.flaky(reruns=N), gets a flaky-test Jira ticket for the BE flaky-test fixer; environment failures such as the instant-container image tests go to DevOps; #integration-tests-nightly gets a weekly green-nights line. cloud-mutation-nightly.yml (17 4 * * *) runs mutmut 3 with tests_dir = tests_api/ on at most 10 rhinoCore files that rhino-ai-agents PRs changed the day before and publishes the survivors as a job summary and an artifact. In cloud-ci.yml and client-ci.yml, integration-tests-aws and -gcp get if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' once the Lab smoke has matched QA for two weeks; the dispatch workflows keep their concurrency groups, and FCP Lab smoke and API Tests become required checks.

tickets.why: A JUnit file per night and the 20-night history table: this lesson.
Triage with the BE guild, the quarantine marker with a ticket, and the weekly green-nights line.
The advisory nightly mutation report on files that agent PRs changed.
Cloud and client branch pushes leave the shared QA locks; QA stays on main, releases and the nightly.

words.plain: A test that passes or fails on the same code, depending on timing or luck.
The standard test report file: one testcase per test, with a failure inside when it failed.
A test that failed, was run again and passed; counted as flaky, not green.
Sorting every failure into real bug, test bug, environment or flaky, each with an owner.
A marker a person adds with a ticket: the test still runs and reports, but cannot turn the night red.
A pytest mark meaning a test is expected to fail; non-strict means a pass is fine too.

review.q: Describe what each pattern in the nightly table usually means: a row that turns red on one date, a row with scattered red, a column with many reds.
review.a: A regression from a change merged that day; a flaky test; an environment problem that hit many tests on one night.

review.q: Why must the history script group JUnit entries by test name?
review.a: pytest-rerunfailures writes one entry per attempt, and retried attempts have no failure element. Grouping lets the last entry be the verdict and the count reveal the rerun.

review.q: What three things make a quarantine safe instead of a way to hide failures?
review.a: The test still runs and reports every night, every quarantine names a ticket with an owner, and only people can add it.

remember: Keep every night per test, count a rerun as flaky, and let a person quarantine with a ticket, so a red night means something new broke.
